subject: chemistry
title: Displacement Reactions
welcome_lead: Reactive metals push less reactive ones out of compounds. Watch the swap happen.
meta_desc: Explore metal displacement reactions in this KS3 chemistry adventure.
final_note: You can now predict which metal will displace another.

concepts.def: A more reactive metal takes the place of a less reactive one.
A metal compound dissolved in water.
Iron displaces copper; solution turns from blue to pale green.
Reactive metal + salt → new salt + displaced metal.
If the metal added is less reactive than the salt's metal.

walkthroughs.body_html:
A more reactive metal can push a less reactive metal out of its compound.

Example: zinc + copper sulfate → zinc sulfate + copper.

Dip an iron nail into blue copper sulfate solution. The nail turns coppery-pink as copper is deposited, and the blue colour fades.

Iron is above copper in the series.
If you put a copper strip in iron sulfate, nothing happens. Copper is below iron in the reactivity series, so it cannot displace iron.

mcqs.q: In 1H NMR, what does the n+1 rule predict?
options: The number of peaks equals the total number of protons in the molecule.
A proton with n equivalent neighbouring protons will appear as a peak split into n+1 sub-peaks.
Splitting tells you how many protons are in the same chemical environment as the one giving the peak.
Positive ions are oxidised at the cathode by losing protons.

mcqs.q: At which electrode are positive ions reduced during electrolysis?
options: Positive ions are reduced at the anode because that's where positive things go.
Positive ions are oxidised at the cathode by losing protons.
At the cathode (the negative electrode) — positive ions gain electrons there.
The number of peaks equals the total number of protons in the molecule.

mcqs.q: Can a single standard electrode potential be measured in isolation?
options: Each electrode has an absolute potential that can be measured directly with a voltmeter.
The number of peaks equals the total number of protons in the molecule.
Standard electrode potentials are measured by submerging the electrode in pure water.
No — electrode potentials are RELATIVE values measured against a reference (the standard hydrogen electrode, defined as 0 V).
